He holds a business degree and a law degree from the University of San Diego. He is a deacon and Sunday school teacher at Park Place Baptist Church and describes his values as conservative.

priorities.text: Says he would encourage parties to work out their own resolutions, including through mediation, while applying the law impartially.
Says landlord-tenant cases have two sides: tenants' need for housing and landlords' obligations to pay taxes, insurance and upkeep.
Says he would handle the docket efficiently and respectfully as the only attorney in the race.

notes.text: In the Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll (769 ballots; not an HBA endorsement), Jack Ezell received 115 votes and Dolores Lozano received 113.
Lists endorsements from True Texas Project and the Texas Home School Coalition.
The Houston Chronicle endorsed his opponent; it reported he initially criticized the court's eviction diversion program and suggested rebranding it as "tenant resources."

q_textualism.summary: Says judges should not try to re-invent the law, which is for lawmakers, and that a judge's job is to apply the law.

issue_notes.summary: Expressed concern that landlords file disproportionately in one of the precinct's two courts; told the Chronicle he was torn on random case assignment.

candidates.current_role: Justice of the Peace, Precinct 2, Place 2, since 2023
candidates.background: Dolores Lozano was elected justice of the peace for Precinct 2, Place 2 in 2022, becoming the first minority and youngest woman to hold the seat, and took office in January 2023. A first-generation college graduate of Baylor University raised in southeast Harris County, she worked as a speech therapist and in civic leadership before taking the bench. She does not hold a law degree, which is not required for the office.

priorities.text: Says she protects the rights of both tenants and small landlords and makes sure every party understands the process and is heard.
Encourages settlement in small claims cases, pausing hearings so parties can resolve disputes.
Is working to persuade fellow justices of the peace to adopt random case assignment, according to the Chronicle.

record.text: Launched an Eviction Diversion Initiative that places a facilitator in the courthouse to connect landlords and tenants with rental assistance, legal aid and mediation; it received a 2024 TAC Best Practice Award.
With Judge Steve Duble, secured a $400,000 national grant for the pilot, which the Chronicle reported cut default judgments by half; the county later took over funding.
Hosts a free legal kiosk at the courthouse that she says is the most used in Texas.

notes.text: The Houston Chronicle editorial board endorsed Dolores Lozano in this race.
In the Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll (769 ballots; not an HBA endorsement), Jack Ezell received 115 votes and Dolores Lozano received 113.
Says she is endorsed by every Democratic member of Harris County Commissioners Court.

candidates.current_role: Justice of the Peace, Precinct 4, Place 2, since 2015
candidates.background: Laryssa Korduba has served as justice of the peace for Harris County Precinct 4, Place 2 since 2015. She holds a law degree, according to the Houston Chronicle. Her 2022 general election was canceled because she was unopposed.

record.text: Handled about 9,000 eviction cases in 2025, compared with 23,800 in the precinct's other court, according to the Chronicle, which reported 6.4 percent of tenants in her court had legal representation.

notes.text: In the Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll (769 ballots; not an HBA endorsement), Laryssa Korduba and Sean Simon each received 106 votes.
Listed as "no response received" in the League of Women Voters of Houston guide; she did not meet with the Chronicle, which endorsed her opponent.

candidates.current_role: Former Justice of the Peace, Precinct 5, Place 1
candidates.background: Mark Fury served two terms as justice of the peace for Precinct 5, Place 1 on Chimney Rock Road in the early 2000s. He says he reduced a 70,000-case backlog in his first five years and that his small claims appeals rate was under half of one percent. He defeated incumbent Judge Bob Wolfe in the 2026 Republican primary and is fully bilingual.

priorities.text: Says he will apply the same approach to small claims that produced a low appeals rate: hearing cases carefully and explaining the applicable law.
Says his ability to conduct eviction trials in Spanish helps tenants and landlords understand each other and the court.
Open to random case assignment to correct caseload imbalances, according to the Chronicle.

promises.text: Committed to performing no weddings during weekday work hours until the court's backlog is addressed, according to the Chronicle.

notes.text: The Houston Chronicle editorial board endorsed Mark Fury in this race.
In the Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll (769 ballots; not an HBA endorsement), Mark Fury received 146 votes and Lisa Jefferson received 107.

candidates.current_role: Chief clerk, Harris County justice of the peace court
candidates.background: Lisa Jefferson is a Houston native and Klein Forest High School graduate who studied criminal justice at Prairie View A&M University. She has worked in Harris County justice of the peace courts since 2012, starting as a court clerk and becoming chief clerk, and has worked with nine judges across five JP courts. She also has more than 15 years of human resources experience.

priorities.text: Plans to have mediators available on the day of court for small claims, with trial the same day if no agreement is reached.
Says she will provide eviction resources to both parties before court, certified translators at every trial and legal aid on site.
Says she will ensure court staff communicate clearly and respectfully so residents understand their cases.

notes.text: In the Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll (769 ballots; not an HBA endorsement), Mark Fury received 146 votes and Lisa Jefferson received 107.

The Houston Chronicle endorsed her opponent; it reported she agreed to random case assignment but also defended landlords' ability to choose a court, and would keep performing weddings on Fridays and weekends.

candidates.current_role: Justice of the Peace, Precinct 8, Place 2, since 1997
candidates.background: Louie Ditta has served as justice of the peace for Harris County Precinct 8, Place 2 since 1997. A Pasadena native, he earned an economics degree from the University of Texas at Austin and a law degree, and previously served as a municipal judge for Pasadena and La Porte. He has served as presiding administrative judge for all 16 Harris County justice courts.

priorities.text: Says he works to make the justice court accessible, efficient and understandable, especially for self-represented parties in small claims and landlord-tenant cases.
Says eviction proceedings require particular attention and that each party should have a meaningful opportunity to be heard.

promises.text: Told the Chronicle he would implement an eviction diversion program if the county funded it.

record.text: Was one of five judges selected to help design the state's Justice Court Reference Manual, according to the Chronicle.

notes.text: The Houston Chronicle editorial board endorsed Louie Ditta in this race.
In the Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll (769 ballots; not an HBA endorsement), Louie Ditta received 162 votes and Nicolas Juan received 72.

The Chronicle reported 93 percent of attorneys responding to the Houston Bar Association evaluation rated him very good or excellent, that his campaign is self-funded, and that fewer than 1 percent of tenants in his court have an attorney.
